/-!
# Erdős Problem 352

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/352](https://www.erdosproblems.com/352)
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped EuclideanGeometry
open scoped ProbabilityTheory

namespace Erdos352

/--
Is there some $c > 0$ such that every measurable $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of measure $\geq c$
 contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_352 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ c > (0: ℝ), ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → ℙ A ≥ c.toEReal
       → (∃ t : Affine.Triangle ℝ ℝ²,
           (∀ p : Fin 3, t.points p ∈ A) ∧
           EuclideanGeometry.triangle_area (t.points 0) (t.points 1) (t.points 2) = 1) := by
  sorry

end Erdos352

reformulations.difference: The source asks for ordinary area 1, whereas EuclideanGeometry.triangle_area is signed and the theorem requires its value to equal +1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The triangle is existentially quantified. An ordinary unit-area triangle has signed area +1 or −1. In the latter case, exchanging vertices 0 and 1 preserves affine independence and membership in A and negates the signed area. Conversely, signed area +1 gives ordinary area 1. This existential equivalence was proved using Affine.Simplex.reindex in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: MeasurableSet on ℝ² uses the Borel sigma-algebra, while the source's measurable sets can be understood as Lebesgue measurable.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every Lebesgue-measurable A contains a Borel subset B with the same volume, including when that volume is infinite. Applying the Lean assertion to B yields triangle vertices in B and hence in A, with the same threshold c. The converse follows because Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable. The fixed-threshold equivalence and the full existential question, also accounting for unsigned area and the measure coercions, were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
